transcript.text: Thanks everyone for being here. As we discussed before, we've got a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit from a former employee, and the complaint is seeking broad inspection of our devices and systems. The case-management conference is next month and no discovery has been exchanged yet. Our priorities are clear: protect the company's confidential information and keep defense costs under control. Before I approve the initial defense plan, I need discovery counsel and insurance-coverage counsel to identify any facts that should shape our approach. What do we need to know to build the right plan? Let's start with discovery counsel -- what are you seeing on your end?

transcript.text: Elena, there's a critical fact that needs to shape our defense plan right now. My forensic review of the former employee's company laptop has been completed. The findings are significant: exactly three identified trade-secret files were confirmed copied to the device. Importantly, the review found no customer data on the laptop and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. This is game-changing for our strategy — it substantially narrows the scope of what the plaintiff can realistically pursue and gives us strong footing to push back against the broad inspection demands in the complaint. I should note the report is still awaiting final partner review and hasn't been added to the case plan yet, but the core findings are solid and should drive our approach to the case-management conference.

transcript.text: Elena, I need to flag several coverage facts that will directly shape our defense plan. I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement, and the trade-secret defense is covered — but with three important conditions. First, there's a $75,000 self-insured retention. Second, we must use insurer-approved panel counsel. Third, we need written insurer consent before engaging any forensic vendor. That last point is critical given Samir's forensic review — we need to confirm whether that vendor engagement had insurer sign-off, because if it didn't, we may have a coverage issue. Also, the endorsement itself is sitting in the risk department's file and hasn't been attached to this matter yet, so we need to get it into the case file. These constraints should factor into our counsel selection and vendor decisions going forward.
